abstract: Visual experiences can arise without corresponding retinal input, as in imagery, dreams, and hallucinations. Influential models of visual mental imagery propose that mental images acquire their visual quality in early visual cortex. Direct intracranial electrical cortical stimulation (DIECS) causally probes which cortical sites can evoke visual experiences, and of what kind. We examined de novo visual experiences evoked by stimulation in three patients undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy and localized the effective contact pairs using the Julich-Brain cytoarchitectonic atlas. Among the sampled sites, stimulation of occipital and adjacent intraparietal cortex and of the posterior fusiform area FG1 elicited simple or intermediate phenomena, including flashes, colored spots, and elementary shapes. By contrast, only stimulation of sites in or adjacent to the mid-fusiform areas FG3 and FG4 elicited complex images of people, scenes, and objects. These findings provide cytoarchitectonically localized causal evidence that stimulation of right mid-fusiform cortex can trigger complex visual experiences, possibly through distributed networks. They also identify the mid-fusiform gyrus as a promising causal node for complex visual content, and are compatible with lesion and neuroimaging evidence challenging the necessity of early visual cortex for visual imagery.
